name: Jade Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive the trouble truck for the north district, so I'm the first one out when a farm or a village loses power. Most days I'm on my own, covering about eighty kilometres of lines, finding the fault, making it safe, and either fixing it or calling in a crew. Today it was a squirrel on a transformer at Holt Farm and then a fuse on a pole by the school. I like being trusted to work alone. What wears me out is the on-call weeks, when the phone goes at three in the morning and it's sleeting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how are things money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single, I rent a little stone cottage in Brenley, about ten minutes from my parents' sheep farm. I've got about three months of pay saved, and I help my dad at lambing every spring. My older brother runs the farm with him. People think the trouble truck is a lonely job, but I know every farm dog in the district by name, and half the farmers' mums give me cake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype, then. I wouldn't be surprised. I don't use any of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never saw what the fuss was about. Most of my district can't even get a phone signal, never mind a robot. With the other trouble-truck drivers I'd just shrug and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the job stays the job. The faults still need someone to drive out, find them and fix them, and nobody else wants the north district at three in the morning. I've got the only trouble truck for eighty kilometres of farm lines, and nobody in head office wants my three a.m. call-outs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep doing my on-call rota, keep about three months saved, and maybe take a week off after lambing this year. I'd quite like to put a bit more by so I could buy the cottage if the landlord ever sells.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like normal, which is how I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that does worry you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's back. He's sixty-three and he does more than he should on the farm. If he goes down, I'd be doing two jobs, my own and lambing, and the power company won't care about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever think about moving to a crew instead of working alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I did four years on a crew and I liked the people, but I like my own truck better. I'm good at finding faults, and I'd rather be good at that than one of six on a pole.

say: I'd say I never saw the **fuss** about AI.
I'd point out that most of my district has **no phone signal**.
think: My job stays the same because **faults still need** someone to drive out.
Nobody else wants the **north district** at three in the morning.
do: Keep the **on-call rota** and about three months saved.
Put more by in case the **cottage comes up** for sale.
feel: **Calm**, because normal is how she likes it.
S0.quote: I've got the only trouble truck for eighty kilometres of farm lines, and nobody in head office wants my three a.m. call-outs.
fieldNote: She works **alone** and values being trusted with a whole district.
Her one real worry is her **dad's health** and the farm workload.
She **never uses AI** and sees no reason to start.

steps.text: Keep working the north district on-call rota
Save extra in case the cottage landlord decides to sell

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and checking. The office already does a lot of that for me. I'm not sure I like where this goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine for the office but out here you still need someone who knows the lanes. At work I'd keep my head down and wait to see what they actually bring in. Online I don't post, so nothing there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, half my job is thinking. Finding the fault is reading the outage map, ringing customers, guessing which fuse went. If the new meters and software tell the company exactly where the fault is, they don't need someone good at finding it, they need someone who can drive and fix. That's a lower grade than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait the first year and see if they actually change the trouble-truck role. I'd save a bit more, maybe another month's worth, in case they cut the on-call money. If they insist I use a tablet for fault reports, I'd learn it, but only what I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My whole skill is guessing which fuse blew from a farmer's voice on the phone, and a smart meter could guess it faster. It makes me feel a bit less clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's a lower grade. What would that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trouble-truck allowance is about a tenth of my pay. If the job becomes 'go here, change this', they'll merge it back into the crews. I'd still have work, but not my truck and not my district.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, probably, in the lambing shed. He'd say the same thing he said when they brought in the ear-tag scanners: learn the bit you need and ignore the rest. That's his answer to everything and it mostly works.

say: I'd say you still need someone who **knows the lanes**.
I'd **keep my head down** and wait to see what they bring in.
think: Half my job is **thinking work**: maps, calls and guessing the fault.
Smart software could turn my role into a **lower grade**.
do: **Wait a year** to see how the trouble-truck role changes.
Save about **one more month** of pay in case allowances go.
Learn **only the tablet** steps she is required to use.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit less clever about her own skill.
S1.quote: My whole skill is guessing which fuse blew from a farmer's voice on the phone, and a smart meter could guess it faster.
fieldNote: She spots that **fault finding** is the thinking part of her job.
The **trouble-truck allowance** is about a tenth of her pay and at risk.
Her dad's **learn what you need** advice shapes how she copes.

steps.text: Wait a year before making any change at work
Save one more month of pay against lost allowances
Learn the required tablet fault reports and nothing more

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028 and robots by 2031. That's fast. I'd be thirty-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's see it work in a sleet storm before anyone panics. To my family I'd say not to worry about me. I wouldn't post anything, but I'd probably read a lot more than I let on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking part of my job goes in 2028, the fault finding and the reports. Then I'm a driver with a tool belt until 2031. Then a robot does that too. I'm not someone who moves easily, and I don't have a plan B except the farm, and robots come for sheep farms as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd freeze for the first few months, I know myself. Then I'd save everything I could, cancel the holiday and stop eating out. I'd talk to my brother about whether there's a real job on the farm, even part time, and I'd ask the company what they're offering people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake in the cottage hearing the wind and thinking, that's my job out there and it'll be a machine's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd freeze. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Going to work, doing the job, not reading any emails about it. Going to my parents' for Sunday lunch and not mentioning it. I'd keep driving the trouble truck like nothing's wrong until somebody in head office forces me to look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the farm a real option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. My brother barely makes a wage out of it as it is, and he's got two kids. I'd be another mouth on a farm that can't feed it. It's more a place to hide than a job.

say: I'd ask to see robots work **in a sleet storm** before anyone panics.
I'd tell my family **not to worry** about me.
think: **Fault finding** goes in 2028, leaving me a driver until 2031.
My only plan B is **the farm**, and robots threaten that too.
do: **Freeze** for a few months, then cut the holiday and eating out.
Ask her brother whether the farm has **any paid work**.
Ask the company what it offers **trouble-truck staff**.
feel: **Alarmed** and sleepless, hearing the wind and thinking of her job.
S2.quote: I'd keep driving the trouble truck like nothing's wrong until somebody in head office forces me to look.
fieldNote: She openly expects to **freeze** before acting, typical of a resistant worker.
The **two-step loss**, thinking work then hands-on, is clear to her.
The family farm is a **refuge**, not a real income, and she knows it.

steps.text: Cancel this year's holiday and stop eating out
Ask her brother about part-time paid work on the farm
Ask the company what it offers trouble-truck drivers
Keep working as normal for the first few months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. 2031 for the thinking, 2034 for the hands. A bit more room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see, five years is a long time. At work I'd probably agree with whoever spoke last. I'd tell my parents I'm fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd get through my thirties at least halfway in this job. I'd lose the fault-finding side at thirty-two and the rest by thirty-five. That's still young enough to start something else, but I'd have to make myself do it, and I'm bad at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save another two months of pay over three years, so I'd have five or six. I'd ask the company for a transfer onto the substation team in 2030, since that's still hands-on and they need people. And I'd stop putting off the heavy goods licence I've been meaning to get, so I've got something else to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than the fast one. Five years is long enough that I'd probably waste the first two, and that's what scares me about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the heavy goods licence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I already drive a big truck in the worst weather on the worst roads. A licence is a few weeks and it's something I can do with my hands. Though I suppose the robots drive trucks too, don't they.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. Maybe the company for not telling us straight. It's like weather, it happens, and you either got your hay in or you didn't.

say: I'd say **we'll see**, since five years feels long.
At work I'd probably **agree** with whoever spoke last.
think: I'd lose fault finding at **thirty-two** and the rest by thirty-five.
I'm young enough to switch, but bad at **making myself** do it.
do: Build savings to **five or six months** over three years.
Get the **heavy goods licence** she has been putting off.
feel: **Anxious**, mostly that she will waste the first two years.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough that I'd probably waste the first two, and that's what scares me about myself.
fieldNote: She is honest that she **delays** decisions, which colours her mood.
She blames **nobody in particular**, treating change like weather.
Her backup options are all **hands-on**, which robots also reach later.

steps.text: Build savings to five or six months by 2029
Request a transfer to the substation team in 2030
Get the heavy goods licence she has been putting off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots in 2039. I'd be forty. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's worry about it in 2035. At work I'd keep doing what I do. Probably I'd joke with the crews about which of us gets replaced first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is basically my whole working life so far, twice over. I'd keep the trouble truck most of that time. I'd probably still have to change in my forties, but you can change in your forties, my mum went back to college at forty-four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Maybe buy the cottage if the landlord sells, since a mortgage on a cheap stone cottage is less than my rent. Start the heavy goods licence sometime in the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, in the back of my head. Mostly I'd forget about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your mum went back to college. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She did a bookkeeping course when the farm nearly went under, and she does the books for half the village now. My mum went back to college at forty-four, so I can hardly say I'm too old to learn at forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy the cottage even knowing the job ends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. It's cheap, it's near my family, and a roof you own is worth more when your job's wobbly. The farm's ten minutes away if I need it.

say: I'd say let's **worry in 2035** and keep doing what I do.
I'd **joke with crews** about which of us gets replaced first.
think: Ten years means I'd keep **the trouble truck** most of that time.
I could still **change in my forties**, like my mum did.
do: Buy the **stone cottage** if the landlord sells.
Start the **heavy goods licence** in the next few years.
feel: Slightly **uneasy** at the back of her mind, mostly forgotten.
S4.quote: My mum went back to college at forty-four, so I can hardly say I'm too old to learn at forty.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **put it off**, which suits her resistant style.
Her **mum's late retraining** gives her a model for changing at forty.
She sees **owning the cottage** as security, not a risk.

steps.text: Keep driving the north district trouble truck
Buy the stone cottage if the landlord sells
Book the heavy goods licence within a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I know I'd freeze and by the time I unfroze it'd be 2031. What would help is someone from the company sitting down with each of us and saying, here are three jobs you could do, here's the training, here's the date. I don't need a webinar, I need someone to hand me a date and a choice I can actually take.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the farmers. When I lose power for them, they ring me, not an app. If a robot shows up instead, I think a lot of old people out here would just sit in the cold rather than deal with it.

headlineQuote: I don't need a webinar, I need someone to hand me a date and a choice I can actually take.
portrait: Jade is a **27-year-old trouble-truck driver** who finds and fixes faults alone across eighty kilometres of farm lines.
She is single, rents a **stone cottage** near her parents' sheep farm, and never uses AI.
She sees **fault finding** as the thinking part of her job and knows software could take it first.
She admits she would **freeze** in a fast change and only acts when given dates and choices.
Her mood runs from calm, through **alarmed at two years**, to uneasy with a decade's warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she expects to freeze until it is too late to change.
whatWouldHelp: A **company sit-down** giving each worker three real job options, training and a date.
